title: Husserl and Phenomenology
subtitle: Back to the things themselves: a science of experience as it is lived
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what phenomenology studies and why Husserl thought philosophy needed it.
By the end you will be able to define intentionality and give everyday examples of it.
By the end you will be able to describe the epoché, or bracketing, and the natural attitude it suspends.
By the end you will be able to explain the lifeworld and Husserl's analysis of time-consciousness.
By the end you will be able to see how phenomenology launched the continental tradition you will study over the next week.
hook:
Paris, around 1932. Three young friends sit in a café on the rue du Montparnasse: Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir and Raymond Aron, who has just returned from studying in Berlin. According to Beauvoir's memoir *The Prime of Life*, Aron pointed to his glass and said something like: you see, if you are a phenomenologist, you can talk about this cocktail and make philosophy out of it. Beauvoir recalls that Sartre turned pale with emotion. This was exactly what he had wanted for years: to describe things as he experienced them, the glass, the drink, the street, and have that count as philosophy.

The method Aron was describing had been invented by a precise, bearded German professor named Edmund Husserl. Over the next week of this course, almost every thinker you meet, Heidegger, Sartre, Beauvoir, Merleau-Ponty, even Derrida, starts from Husserl, whether to follow him or to argue against him. Today you learn the method that set them all going.

sections.heading: A Mathematician in Search of Foundations
sections.body:
Edmund Husserl was born in 1859 in Prossnitz, in Moravia (today Prostějov in the Czech Republic), into a Jewish family; he later converted to Lutheran Christianity. He trained as a mathematician, writing a doctorate on the calculus of variations, but in Vienna in the 1880s he attended the lectures of the philosopher and former priest Franz Brentano, and the experience changed his life. Philosophy, Brentano convinced him, could be a rigorous science.

Husserl's first big project was about the foundations of arithmetic. What are numbers, and how do we know truths about them? A popular answer at the time was **psychologism**: logic and mathematics are really just descriptions of how human minds happen to think. Husserl at first leaned that way, and Frege (Day 69) criticised him for it. In his breakthrough work, the *Logical Investigations* (1900–1901), Husserl turned decisively against psychologism. The truth that 2 + 2 = 4 is not a fact about anyone's brain; it would hold even if no one ever thought it. Yet we do grasp such truths in conscious acts. How?

That question pushed him toward a new discipline: a careful description of the structures of consciousness itself, of how things show up for us. He called it **phenomenology**, from the Greek *phainomenon*, that which appears. Phenomenology is not psychology, which studies the mind as one more natural object with causes and effects. It studies experience from the inside, exactly as it is lived, aiming to capture its essential structures. Husserl summed up the spirit of the movement with a rallying cry: *Zu den Sachen selbst!*, back to the things themselves. Stop theorising about experience from a distance; look at what actually appears and describe it faithfully.

Husserl taught at Göttingen and then, from 1916, at Freiburg, where he gathered brilliant students, including Edith Stein and a young Martin Heidegger.

sections.heading: Intentionality: Consciousness Is Always Of Something
sections.body:
Husserl's starting point came from Brentano: the idea of **intentionality**. In philosophy, this word does not mainly mean doing something on purpose. It means *directedness* or *aboutness*. Every conscious act is directed at something. You never simply see; you see *a tree*. You never simply fear; you fear *the dog*, or the exam. You remember *your grandmother's kitchen*, imagine *a unicorn*, hope *for rain*. Consciousness always points beyond itself.

This sounds obvious, but it has big consequences. Recall Descartes on Day 43: he pictured the mind as a sealed inner theatre, privately watching ideas, and then had the huge problem of how to get from those ideas to the outside world. Husserl suggests that the starting point was wrong. Consciousness is not a box with pictures in it; it is, from the start, a reaching-out toward things.

Husserl added a crucial distinction. In every intentional experience there is the act itself, which he called the *noesis* (the seeing, remembering, judging), and the object *as it is meant* in that act, the *noema*. The same object can be meant in very different ways. You can think of Venus as *the morning star* or as *the evening star*, as Frege noticed (Day 69); you can perceive a house, remember it, or imagine moving into it. Phenomenology studies these different modes of givenness.

Take perception. When you look at a coffee cup, you only ever see one side of it. Yet you do not experience a flat, one-sided surface; you experience a cup, with a hidden back and a bottom you cannot see. Husserl says the hidden sides are *co-intended*: anticipated as part of what you perceive, ready to be confirmed (or surprised) as you turn the cup. He called this background of expectations a **horizon**. Every perception is surrounded by horizons of what could be seen next, and of the wider world in which the object sits.

Husserl also distinguished between **empty** and **fulfilled** intentions. Suppose a friend tells you about a restaurant: you can think about its famous chocolate cake, mean it, even crave it, while it is given only emptily, in words. When you finally sit down and taste it, your intention is *fulfilled*: the very thing you meant is now given in person. Knowledge, for Husserl, is fundamentally this experience of fulfilment, the match between what we meant and what shows up. A disappointing cake is a partial fulfilment: it is the cake you meant, but not as you meant it. This gave him a way to talk about truth not as a mysterious correspondence between a mind and a world on the other side of a wall, but as something we live through every day, as expectations are confirmed, corrected or overturned.

sections.heading: The Epoché: Putting the World in Brackets
sections.body:
How do you study experience itself, rather than the things experienced? In *Ideas I* (1913), Husserl introduced his central method. In everyday life we live in the **natural attitude**: we simply take for granted that the world exists out there, that the table is solid, that other people have minds, that science describes reality. We are absorbed in things and never notice the experiencing that gives them to us.

Husserl asks us to perform an **epoché**, borrowing a word from the ancient Skeptics (Day 27), who used it for suspending judgement. Phenomenologists also call it **bracketing**. We do not deny that the world exists, like a radical sceptic, nor doubt it, like Descartes. We simply set aside the question of its existence, put it in brackets, so that we can attend to how the world is given to consciousness. Instead of asking *is this table real?*, we ask *how does this table show up for me: as solid, as brown, as something to lean on, as continuing behind my back?*

A helpful comparison: a painter learning to paint a white plate on a sunny table must stop seeing *white plate* and start seeing the yellows, blues and greys that actually appear. The painter does not deny the plate is white; she brackets that knowledge to see what is given. Husserl wanted to do something similar, but for all of experience, including thought, memory, emotion and our sense of other people.

Husserl went further with a method called **eidetic variation**, from the Greek *eidos*, essence or form (Plato's word on Day 11). To find the essence of, say, a melody, you imagine varying it: change the key, the instrument, the tempo. What can you change while it remains the same melody, and what can you not change? The features that survive all variations are its essential structure.

Critics found the epoché hard to perform, and Husserl's own students argued about what it achieves. In his middle period he drifted toward what he called **transcendental idealism**, treating the world as constituted by consciousness, a move many followers, including Heidegger and Edith Stein, refused to make.

sections.heading: Time, the Body and Other People
sections.body:
Some of Husserl's most beautiful descriptions concern our experience of **time**. Listen to a melody. At any instant you hear only one note. Yet you do not experience a sequence of isolated notes; you hear a tune. How?

Husserl's answer: the living present is not a knife-edge instant. Each moment of experience contains a **retention** of what has just passed (the previous note, still held, fading) and a **protention**, an anticipation of what is about to come (the next note you expect). That is why a wrong note jars: your protention was disappointed. This is not memory, which is a deliberate calling-up of the past, but a structure built into every moment of awareness. Remember Augustine on Day 31, wondering how time could be measured in the mind? Husserl, who lectured on Augustine, thought he had finally described the structure Augustine glimpsed.

Husserl also described the **lived body**. Your body is not just one physical object among others. It is the place from which you perceive, the *here* around which everything else is *there*. When your left hand touches your right, each is both touching and touched, a strange doubling that no ordinary object has. His French reader Maurice Merleau-Ponty built a whole philosophy on this in *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945), arguing that we are not minds steering bodies but embodied beings whose understanding of the world lives in our skills and gestures. A typist's fingers know the keyboard without the typist being able to say where the letters are.

And how do we experience other people? In the *Cartesian Meditations* (based on lectures given in Paris in 1929), Husserl tried to show how we grasp another body as another *lived* body, a centre of experience like ourselves, through what he called **empathy** (*Einfühlung*). His student Edith Stein had written her doctoral dissertation on this very problem of empathy in 1916. Many readers feel Husserl never fully escaped the solitary starting point he inherited from Descartes, but he opened questions about intersubjectivity that the next generation took up eagerly.

sections.heading: The Lifeworld and a Philosopher's Last Years
sections.body:
Husserl's last great work, *The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology* (begun 1936), was written in darkening times. After 1933 the Nazi regime's laws stripped him, as a man of Jewish birth, of his university privileges; his licence to teach was withdrawn, and he could no longer publish in Germany; the first parts of the *Crisis* appeared in 1936 in a journal in Belgrade. His former student and successor at Freiburg, Martin Heidegger, whom you will meet tomorrow, became rector of the university that same year and joined the Nazi Party. Heidegger had dedicated *Being and Time* to Husserl in 1927; the dedication was dropped from a 1941 edition.

In the *Crisis*, Husserl argued that modern science, since Galileo (Day 41), had brought astonishing power but also a kind of forgetting. Galileo mathematized nature: real things became quantities and equations, while colours, warmth and meaning were treated as merely subjective. Science forgot its own roots in the **lifeworld** (*Lebenswelt*): the everyday world of lived experience, of tables, faces, weather and tasks, which all scientific concepts ultimately come from and must answer to. A physicist's measurements are made with eyes and hands in a laboratory that is part of the lifeworld. When science forgets this, Husserl warned, it loses its connection to the questions of meaning that matter to human beings, and Europe, he thought, was suffering a crisis of meaning as a result.

Husserl died in Freiburg in 1938. He left behind some 40,000 pages of shorthand manuscripts. A young Belgian Franciscan priest, Herman Van Breda, smuggled them out of Nazi Germany to Leuven, where the Husserl Archives still publish them. Edith Stein, who had become a Catholic nun, was murdered at Auschwitz in 1942.

Phenomenology's legacy is enormous. It shaped existentialism, hermeneutics, much of continental philosophy, and today's cognitive science of embodiment. Its central claim remains challenging: before we theorise about the world, we should look carefully at how it actually appears.

modernConnection.title: Neurophenomenology and the Science of Experience
modernConnection.body:
Brain scanners can now show which regions of the brain light up when you see a face, feel pain or remember a holiday. But a brain scan, on its own, says nothing about what the experience is *like*. A neuroscientist studying pain needs subjects to report their pain: sharp or dull, throbbing or steady, frightening or bearable. In other words, the science of consciousness depends on descriptions of lived experience, and those descriptions can be careless or careful. That is the opening Husserl would have predicted.

In the 1990s the Chilean neuroscientist Francisco Varela proposed **neurophenomenology**: pairing brain imaging with disciplined first-person reports, using training inspired by phenomenology and by meditation practice. In one well-known study, Varela's group, led by Antoine Lutz, trained participants to describe in detail how ready and focused they felt before each trial of a visual task, and found that those reports helped make sense of variations in their brain activity that would otherwise have looked like noise. Experience, carefully described, turned out to be data.

Phenomenology has also moved into medicine. Philosophers such as Havi Carel, who lives with a serious lung disease, use Husserl's and Merleau-Ponty's tools to describe what illness is like from the inside: how breathlessness shrinks the horizon of possibilities, making a staircase into a mountain. Doctors trained only in the natural attitude, focused on measurable symptoms, can miss this lived dimension.

The comparison has limits. Husserl wanted to uncover *essential* structures of all possible experience, not run experiments, and he would have resisted turning phenomenology into a tool of neuroscience. Many scientists, meanwhile, distrust introspection as unreliable. But the core lesson holds: you cannot have a complete science of the mind that leaves out how things appear to the one who has it. You will meet this problem again on Day 84 with Nagel's bat and the hard problem of consciousness.

vocabulary.definition: The philosophical study of the structures of experience and consciousness, as they are lived from the first-person point of view.
vocabulary.example: A phenomenology of waiting would describe how time drags, how attention keeps turning to the door, and how every sound seems significant.

vocabulary.definition: The directedness or aboutness of consciousness: every conscious act is of or about something.
vocabulary.example: Your worry is not just a feeling floating free; it is about tomorrow's interview, which shows its intentionality.

vocabulary.definition: Husserl's term for our ordinary, unreflective assumption that the world simply exists out there as it appears.
vocabulary.example: When you reach for your phone without wondering whether it is real, you are in the natural attitude.

vocabulary.definition: The phenomenological method of suspending judgement about the existence of the world in order to focus on how things are given in experience.
vocabulary.example: Bracketing whether the ghost in the story is real, the phenomenologist describes how the dark hallway feels threatening.

vocabulary.definition: The background of anticipated but not currently given aspects that surrounds every perception.
vocabulary.example: When you see the front of a house, its back rooms belong to the horizon of your perception.

vocabulary.definition: Husserl's terms for the just-past held in present awareness and the about-to-come anticipated in it, which together make experience of time possible.
vocabulary.example: You can hear a sentence as a sentence because earlier words are retained and the ending is protended.

vocabulary.definition: The body as experienced from within, as the centre of perception and action rather than as one physical object among others.
vocabulary.example: When you reach for a cup without looking, you rely on your lived body's sense of where your hand is.

vocabulary.definition: The everyday world of lived experience that forms the background and foundation of all theoretical and scientific activity.
vocabulary.example: Before a chemist knows water as H₂O, she lives with water in the lifeworld as something to drink and wash with.

thinkingExercise.title: Five Minutes of Bracketing
thinkingExercise.prompt: Try a small phenomenological description of an ordinary experience, and notice how much you normally overlook.
steps: Choose a simple object or activity within reach: a cup of tea, the view from a window, the sound of rain, washing your hands.
For three minutes, bracket every theory about it (what it is made of, its price, its causes). Write only how it appears: colours, textures, sounds, what is hidden, what you expect next.
Identify its horizon: which aspects are not given but anticipated? Turn or move the object if you can. Were your anticipations confirmed?
Notice the time structure. What are you retaining from a moment ago, and what are you protending?
Reflect in a paragraph: did bracketing reveal anything? Is it truly possible to set aside the natural attitude, or did theories keep creeping back in?

summary: Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) founded phenomenology, the rigorous description of experience as it is lived, under the slogan *back to the things themselves*.
Following Brentano, he made intentionality central: consciousness is always directed at something, and the same object can be given in many ways.
The epoché, or bracketing, suspends the natural attitude so that we can describe how the world is given to consciousness rather than debating whether it exists.
Husserl analysed time-consciousness (retention and protention), the lived body, empathy and the lifeworld that underlies all science.
Persecuted under Nazism, Husserl left a huge legacy: Heidegger, Sartre, Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty all began from phenomenology.

quiz.question: What does intentionality mean in Husserl's phenomenology?
options: Doing things deliberately
The ability to plan for the future
The directedness of consciousness toward an object
The freedom of the will
quiz.explanation: Following Brentano, Husserl uses intentionality for the aboutness of every conscious act: seeing is of something, fearing is of something.

quiz.question: What is the epoché?
options: Suspending judgement about the world's existence to describe how it is given in experience
Denying that the external world exists
Doubting everything until certainty is reached
A historical period of Greek thought
quiz.explanation: Husserl's bracketing neither denies nor doubts the world; it sets the question of existence aside to focus on appearances.

quiz.question: Husserl's *Logical Investigations* defended psychologism, the view that logic is just a description of how human minds happen to think.
quiz.explanation: The *Logical Investigations* (1900–1901) famously attacked psychologism; logical truths hold regardless of anyone's psychology.

quiz.question: You look at the front of a cereal box and take for granted that it has a back. In Husserl's terms, the unseen back belongs to the perception's...
options: noesis
epoché
retention
horizon
quiz.explanation: The horizon is the background of co-intended but not currently given aspects that surrounds every perception.

quiz.question: Why does a wrong note in a familiar song jar us, according to Husserl's analysis of time?
options: Because memory has failed
Because our protention, our anticipation of what comes next, is disappointed
Because the ear cannot process sound sequences
Because of the natural attitude
quiz.explanation: Every present moment includes protention of what is to come; a wrong note frustrates that built-in anticipation.

quiz.question: In the *Crisis of European Sciences*, what did Husserl say modern science had forgotten?
options: Its roots in the lifeworld of everyday experience
The importance of mathematics
The existence of God
The laws of logic
quiz.explanation: Husserl argued that since Galileo, science had mathematized nature and forgotten that all its concepts arise from and answer to the lifeworld.

quiz.question: The ancient Skeptics had used the word *epoché* for suspending judgement long before Husserl.
quiz.explanation: Husserl borrowed the term from the ancient Skeptics (Day 27), though he gave it a new methodological role.

quiz.question: Which modern research approach is most directly inspired by Husserl's phenomenology?
options: Behaviourist psychology, which ignores inner experience
Neurophenomenology, which combines brain imaging with disciplined first-person reports
Machine translation
Public opinion polling
quiz.explanation: Francisco Varela's neurophenomenology explicitly draws on phenomenological methods to make careful descriptions of experience into scientific data.

quiz.question: What happened to Husserl's manuscripts after his death in 1938?
options: They were burned by the Nazis
Heidegger published them under his own name
Herman Van Breda smuggled them to Leuven, where the Husserl Archives were founded
They were lost until the 1990s
quiz.explanation: The Franciscan Herman Van Breda rescued around 40,000 pages of shorthand manuscripts and brought them to Leuven in Belgium.

quiz.question: Merleau-Ponty developed Husserl's idea of the lived body into a philosophy in which we are embodied beings rather than minds steering machines.
quiz.explanation: His *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945) argued that understanding lives in bodily skills and perception.

goDeeper.body:
Husserl's career is often divided into phases, and scholars fiercely debate how they fit together. The *Logical Investigations* seemed to many early readers, especially the Munich and Göttingen circles, to be a realist work: describe things themselves, as they are given. Then came *Ideas I* (1913) with its **transcendental turn**: the phenomenological reduction leads back to a transcendental ego, a pure consciousness that constitutes the meaning of the world. Many of his students felt betrayed, seeing a slide into idealism like Kant's (Day 55) or worse, Berkeley's (Day 48). Husserl insisted this was a misreading: constitution is not creation, and transcendental idealism is meant to explain how the world comes to have meaning for us, not to deny its reality. Interpreters such as Dan Zahavi have argued that Husserl's idealism is closer to a theory of meaning than to metaphysical idealism.

A second debate concerns whether the **epoché can ever be completed**. Merleau-Ponty wrote in the preface to *Phenomenology of Perception* that the most important lesson the reduction teaches us is the impossibility of a complete reduction. We are always already in the world, embodied and embedded; we can loosen our grip on the natural attitude, but never step entirely outside it. Heidegger went further, arguing that Husserl had focused on consciousness and knowledge while neglecting the more basic question of what it is to *be* the kind of entity that has a world at all. That is where tomorrow's lesson begins.

Finally, there is the analytic connection. Husserl and Frege corresponded, and their theories of meaning (noema and sense) are strikingly parallel, which suggests the later split between analytic and continental philosophy was not inevitable.

readings.title: Cartesian Meditations
readings.author: Edmund Husserl
readings.note: Husserl's own short introduction to phenomenology, based on his 1929 Paris lectures; demanding but the most compact primary source.

readings.title: Introduction to Phenomenology
readings.author: Robert Sokolowski
readings.note: A wonderfully clear guide using everyday examples like cubes and photographs; the best place for a beginner to start.

readings.title: At the Existentialist Café
readings.author: Sarah Bakewell
readings.note: A lively group biography that opens with the apricot cocktail story and explains Husserl's influence on Sartre, Beauvoir and Heidegger.

readings.title: Phenomenology of Perception
readings.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
readings.note: For the ambitious: read the preface on what phenomenology is, then the chapters on the body.

questions: Can we ever describe experience without already interpreting it through language and theory?
Is a first-person description of experience a legitimate kind of evidence in science? When should we trust it?
Husserl thought modern science had lost touch with the lifeworld. Do you see signs of that today, or is the complaint exaggerated?
